Pulitzer Prize- winning Hernon Diaz spoke globally about his new novel Ply , and its foray into that ever-so-fraught topic of technology. Susan Orlean and Jayne Anne Phillips together weighed in on the writing of memoirs, with Orleans, a New Yorker sta writer and author, viewing her Joy R id e as a “turning of the lens.” Phillips approached her work as a chronicle of “what I’ve loved, what I’ve lost, what I’ve witnessed, what’s been really impor- tant to me,” connecting it also with her acclaimed novel Night Watch . Belle Burden, author of S t r a n g e r s , revealed her own trajectory to telling much about her abruptly upended marriage. There was shop talk, too. Jenna Bush Hager got under the hood of today’s pub- lishing world with Tiger’s Mouth author Lucy Tan, who is published by Hager’s imprint. Angel Down novelist Daniel Kraus recounted holding fast to his WWI setting in spite of the marketing appeal of World War II. And there were plenty of laughs, too. Jones reected on “the tyranny of 1950s undergarments” seen in Sears, Roebuck & Co. catalogs. Curtis Sittenfeld, author of Show Don’t Tell: Stories , which con- nects two decades later with her famed novel P r e p , “Whether you nd group hugs excruciating or like delightful … is a very revealing fact about a person.” But through hell or high-ticket demand, the connective thread of timely, vital ideas converging in the Charleston Literary Festival’s curatorial vision for 10 days is a lifeline, too, whether washing over the historic Charleston theater seats or through one revelatory link after another, all coming to a cozy sofa near you.
